analysis.one_liner: Caps House campaign spending and gives public matching funds to candidates who accept the limits.
analysis.headline: The bill went to three House committees in February 1993, was sent to two subcommittees, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill set up a voluntary system for House campaigns: a candidate who agrees to spend no more than $600,000 (and no more than $400,000 in the general election) would get public matching funds of up to $400,000 for small donations from individuals. It capped contributions from political committees and large donors at $200,000, barred candidates from spending more than $50,000 of their own money, required national parties to bring their unregulated 'soft money' under federal contribution limits and disclosure rules, and tightened rules on independent expenditures, disclosure thresholds, and ad sponsorship statements. It also required broadcasters to sell candidates airtime at the lowest rate and not preempt it, restricted taxpayer-funded mass mailings by members to their own districts, and required candidates receiving benefits to take part in at least one public debate.
analysis.who_benefits: Challengers and candidates without personal wealth or access to large donors, who could run competitive campaigns on public matching funds tied to small individual contributions. Voters also gain from fuller disclosure of soft money, faster reporting of late independent spending, and ads that clearly name who paid for them.

how_it_helps.text: Eligible House candidates receive up to $400,000 in public matching funds, at two dollars for every one dollar raised from individuals giving $250 or less [S2][S3].

Candidates who accept the program face $600,000 spending and contribution limits, a $50,000 cap on personal funds, and $200,000 caps on contributions from political committees and from large donors [S2][S3].

National, state, and local party committees must bring all money connected in whole or part to federal elections under federal limits and reporting, and national parties may not solicit contributions exempt from those rules — closing the 'soft money' channel [S2][S3].

Disclosure is broadened: the reporting threshold for non-committee donors drops from $200 to $50, late independent expenditures of $1,000 or more must be reported within 24 hours, and advertising must carry a clearly readable sponsorship statement, with the candidate on camera or on mic saying they approved the message [S2][S3].
Members may not use official funds for mass mailings outside their own district, ending taxpayer-funded newsletters that reach beyond the constituents a member represents [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Broadcasters, who must sell candidate ads at their lowest rate during the final weeks before elections and cannot preempt them; political parties and large donors, who lose the unregulated soft money and contribution channels; and self-funded wealthy candidates, whose personal spending advantage triggers extra matching funds for opponents. Taxpayers fund the matching system, which the bill requires to be budget-neutral.
analysis.who_pays_short: Broadcasters, parties, big donors, wealthy self-funders

drawbacks.text: The Supreme Court had held in Buckley v. Valeo that mandatory limits on candidate campaign spending violate the First Amendment; this bill works around that by making limits voluntary with public benefits attached, but its spending caps on nonparticipating candidates' reporting and its express-advocacy rules for independent spending remained open to constitutional challenge — the bill itself provides expedited Supreme Court review anticipating that fight [S3].

Broadcasters objected that lowest-unit-rate rules combined with a ban on preemption force them to carry political ads at below-market prices in their most valuable weeks, a compelled-speech and property-rights objection [S2][S3].

Spending limits can cut both ways: limits pegged to national averages are generous enough for cheap media markets but tight in expensive ones, and matching funds depend on the Federal Election Commission certifying payments quickly — a commission the bill itself notes needs stronger enforcement authority [S2][S3].

An opponent who refuses to participate can still spend freely, and the bill's waivers (which unlock limits once a nonparticipating opponent crosses 80 percent of the spending limit) invite arm-race dynamics that could pressure candidates into opting out entirely [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is public money and below-rate airtime in exchange for lower campaign spending and cleaner disclosure. The voluntary design answers the main constitutional objection to spending caps, and the soft money and disclosure provisions attack loopholes that had real-world effects on who could run and what voters could see. The serious costs are the taxpayer price of matching funds (offset by design but real), the burden on broadcasters, and the risk that a voluntary system only works if most candidates in a race opt in — otherwise the waivers make limits easy to escape. On balance it was a substantial, if complex, attempt to reduce money's role in House elections.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced, sent to two subcommittees, and then simply sat there until Congress ended with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ben Cardin introduced the Congressional Campaign Reform Act of 1993 on February 4, 1993 [S5][S1].
The same day, it was referred to three committees: House Administration, Energy and Commerce, and Post Office and Civil Service [S5].
On February 11 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Postal Operations and Services, and on February 24 to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and Finance [S5].
No further action appears in the record; the bill had one cosponsor (a Democrat) and died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S4][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress, the political parties, large donors, and broadcasters kept the campaign finance status quo — unlimited soft money for parties, no spending limits, and no expanded disclosure — because the bill never advanced out of committee.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only Democratic sponsorship (the sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor) and no votes, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill forces stations to sell candidate airtime at the lowest rate for the same time slot and bars them from preempting candidate ads, cutting into their most profitable ad inventory. Their interest in the bill ran against the voters who would see candidates' messages at affordable rates.

industries.industry: Political parties (national, state, and local committees)
industries.note: The bill brings soft money — money raised outside federal limits for activities partly connected to federal elections — under federal limits, disclosure, and reporting rules, and caps what state parties can spend on federal-presidential campaigns. Parties had relied on this unregulated money as their main big-donor pipeline.

industries.industry: Large individual donors and political action committees
industries.note: House candidates could accept no more than $200,000 in combined contributions from political committees and from donors giving over $250, shrinking the weight of big money in House races.

industries.industry: Wealthy self-funded candidates and incumbent members of Congress
industries.note: Candidates are capped at $50,000 of personal funds, with opponents getting tripled matching funds if a self-funder exceeds that; incumbents with over $600,000 banked must move the excess out of their campaign accounts for their own races. These provisions target the two groups with the biggest built-in money advantages in House elections.

Credit extended by advertising and mass-mail vendors becomes a reportable contribution if over $1,000 and over 60 days, tightening their role, but candidates receiving public funds must still buy their services, and fundraising costs are partly exempt from spending limits.
